tier_reason: benchmarks/ReadMe.md compares hpp-proto directly with Google protobuf 33.2 using public code (benchmarks/benchmark.cpp, Google Benchmark, built by benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt) and states the compilers (Apple clang 17.0.0, gcc 13.3.0) and CPUs (M1 Pro, i9-11950H). No optimization flags or build type are stated for the published numbers: the page's own run command (`cmake -B build -DHPP_PROTO_BENCHMARKS=ON`) sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, and only an unlinked 'benchmark' preset in CMakePresets.json sets Release. That rules out A, and first-party numbers are C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Linux numbers from the README prose (i9-11950H, gcc 13.3.0, protobuf 33.2). Deserialize, google arena vs hpp-proto non-owning: proto2 210 ns vs 141 ns (~1.5x), proto3 252 ns vs 160 ns (~1.6x). Deserialize regular: proto2 215 vs 210 ns, proto3 251 vs 212 ns. repeated_packed: google regular 4164 ns vs hpp-proto regular 2624 ns (~1.6x); google arena 4263 ns vs hpp-proto non-owning 2550 ns. Set_message+serialize, google arena vs hpp-proto non-owning: proto2 186 vs 99.6 ns (~1.9x), proto3 223 vs 121 ns (~1.8x); regular: proto2 185 vs 139 ns, proto3 219 vs 148 ns. Google is faster on serialize-only: proto2 64.5 vs 85.1 ns, proto3 98.8 vs 102 ns. (Ratios derived from page data.)
corrections.workload: Google Benchmark (benchmarks/benchmark.cpp) runs deserialize, set_message, serialize-only and set_message+serialize. It uses GoogleMessage1 (proto2 and proto3) from the protobuf v3.6.0 benchmarks.proto schema, with a single ~220-byte message filled in code by set_message_google, not the v3.6.0 dataset files. There is also a 'big' variant with 512- and 2048-byte strings, and a 1000-element packed repeated uint64 message with random values. Google protobuf runs in regular and arena modes; hpp-proto runs in regular and non-owning modes.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 17.0.0 (Mac); gcc 13.3.0 (Linux); Google protobuf 33.2. Optimization flags and build type are not stated for the published results. The ReadMe run command sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE; CMakePresets.json has a 'benchmark' preset with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, but it is not tied to the published numbers.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark. Flags and build type are not stated for the published numbers. The README prose numbers do not exactly match the committed benchmarks/Linux_bench.result. For example, in the raw file repeated_packed takes 3966 ns wall / 3852 ns CPU for google regular (the prose says 4164) and 2650 / 2511 ns for hpp-proto regular (the prose says 2624). The workload is one small in-code GoogleMessage1 plus synthetic packed data, not the v3.6.0 dataset files. Google wins serialize-only (proto2 64.5 vs 85.1 ns). The headline gains compare hpp-proto non-owning mode with Google arena mode; in regular deserialize mode the gap is small (proto2 215 vs 210 ns). The Mac (M1 Pro) results have the same shape. Only two machines were tested, with no variance reported.

notes: The numbers match benchmarks/ReadMe.md (Linux section). The main branch's last commit is 2026-08-03; the 2026-09-25 date comes from a non-default cflite-corpus branch. If the orchestrator accepts the CMakePresets.json 'benchmark' preset (Release) as the stated flags, the entry would meet A, but the page itself states no flags.

tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed SOSP 2023 paper (DOI 10.1145/3600006.3613137). Tables 1-3 and Figure 7 compare Cornflakes with Protobuf, FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto on stated hardware (EPYC 7402P, CloudLab c6525-100g, ConnectX-5Ex), and the code is public (cf-kv/, ds-echo/). The Cargo.toml release profile gives the flags, but the rustc version is not pinned: install/install-rust.sh installs 1.70.0 and then runs `rustup default stable`. The paper states no compiler, so it is not A, and B stands.

corrections.claimed_speedup: CDN image trace (Table 2), in thousands of objects/s: Cornflakes 366.5 vs Cap'n Proto 161.0, FlatBuffers 181.2 and Protobuf 186.1; the paper says 97-128% higher. Twitter cache trace (Fig. 7): 15.4-45.9% higher throughput than the three baselines, at a p99 of 52 us for Cornflakes vs 53 us (FlatBuffers, Protobuf) and 61 us (Cap'n Proto). Google bytes-size trace (Table 1), in thousands of req/s: no win for small values. Cornflakes has 844.7 vs Protobuf 852.5 (1 value) and 727.2 vs 741.9 (1-4 values). It leads only at 1-8 values (584.5 vs 583.8) and 1-16 values (441.2 vs 412.0). Redis (Table 3) is measured against Redis's own handwritten serialization, not Protobuf, FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto: 15-40.1% higher throughput (get 23.37 vs 18.49 Gbps, mget-2 14.12 vs 12.27, lrange-2 15.07 vs 10.75).
corrections.baseline: Protobuf, FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto via the pure-Rust crates protobuf 3.0.3 (rust-protobuf), flatbuffers 2.1.2 and capnp 0.13.6 (cf-kv/Cargo.toml); Redis handwritten serialization for Table 3
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc version not pinned: install/install-rust.sh installs 1.70.0 and then runs `rustup default stable`. Cargo.toml [profile.release] sets opt-level=3, lto="fat", codegen-units=1, panic="abort"; the Makefile builds with --release unless DEBUG=y. The paper states no compiler.
corrections.caveats: The baselines are pure-Rust implementations (rust-protobuf 3.0.3, the flatbuffers 2.1.2 Rust runtime, capnproto-rust 0.13.6), not wrappers around the canonical C++ libraries. The C++ installs in install/install-libraries.sh are used only for the protoc/flatc/capnp code generators. All systems run over Cornflakes's own kernel-bypass UDP stack, with a per-library network API. There is no gain on small-object workloads (Table 1: within 98% of Protobuf at 1 and 1-4 values). The Redis gains are against Redis's handwritten serialization. The rustc version is not pinned. The repo has no LICENSE file. The default branch's last commit is 2023-07-27; a non-default 'timetrace' branch has a commit from 2024-01-19.

notes: The paper's numbers are quoted correctly. The record's caveat that the Rust crates 'wrap each C/C++ library' was wrong: all three are pure-Rust runtimes, per cf-kv/Cargo.toml. The last commit on the default branch (main) is 2023-07-27, more than 3 years ago, so the status is abandoned; the 2024-01-19 date is from the timetrace branch. The license is null with no LICENSE file, so 'reference' is correct.

tier_reason: The jviotti/binary-json-size-benchmark README tables do show Bond Compact Binary v1 smaller than FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto. The code is public (benchmark/<doc>/bond/, Makefile) and the tool versions are pinned in DEPENDENCIES. But this is a small suite (26 stars, archived) run by the author of a competing format (JSON BinPack), and its arXiv write-up (2201.03051) is an unrefereed preprint. So it is not a well-known independent suite, and no compiler, flags or CPU are stated. That makes it C, matching how this wave tiered JSON BinPack and the CppSerialization suite.

corrections.workload: Uncompressed encoded byte size of 27 real-world JSON documents (SchemaStore test-suite samples), each re-encoded with the format's own schema. The quoted cases are the JSON Resume example (3,048 bytes as minified JSON, per the page's JSON row) and CircleCI Definition (Blank) (14 bytes as JSON).
corrections.claimed_speedup: JSON Resume: Bond Compact Binary v1 is 2256 bytes vs FlatBuffers 3116 (~28% smaller), Cap'n Proto binary 3152 (~28% smaller) and Cap'n Proto packed 2549 (~11% smaller). Protobuf is smaller than Bond at 2225 bytes. CircleCI-blank: Bond 10 bytes vs FlatBuffers 20 and Cap'n Proto binary 24; packed Cap'n Proto is 6 and Protobuf 5. Across all 27 documents, Bond is smaller than FlatBuffers on 27/27, than binary Cap'n Proto on 26/27 and than packed Cap'n Proto on 21/27, but smaller than Protobuf on only 1/27 (geojson). The benchmark measures size only, not speed. (Percentages and counts derived from page data.)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 2.6k stars (2,620, microsoft/bond); the open-source project ended in March 2025 and the repo is archived
corrections.caveats: Size-only benchmark with no CPU time. It is run by Juan Cruz Viotti, author of the competing JSON BinPack format, as a small suite (26 stars). It was archived in Nov 2023 and superseded by benchmark.sourcemeta.com, which no longer includes Bond. The tool versions are stated (Bond C++ 9.0.4, capnp 0.8.0, flatc 1.12.0, protobuf 3.15.3); no compiler, flags or CPU are stated. The arXiv write-up 2201.03051 is an unrefereed preprint. Protobuf is smaller than Bond on 26 of 27 documents, and Thrift, Avro and ASN.1 PER are usually smaller as well. The win holds only against FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto. Results vary per document; the page has 27 documents, not ~24.

notes: The quoted numbers match the page, but the record's '~2.1KB source JSON' was wrong: minified it is 3,048 bytes. The baseline choice (FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto) hides that Protobuf beats Bond on size in almost every document. The metadata is confirmed: MIT license, archived, last commit 2025-04-01, abandoned.
